comorbidity and medicines modify risk.

steps.test: Serum creatinine with estimated glomerular filtration rate
steps.clinical_question: Is reduced kidney function present and persistent?
steps.expected_finding: Use creatinine-based eGFR in adults; a new eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² should be repeated to confirm the result.
steps.decision_rationale: NICE uses eGFR to detect and classify reduced kidney function while recognising biological and analytical variability.
steps.timeframe: Repeat a new eGFR below 60 within 2 weeks; use serial results to establish chronicity and progression

steps.clinical_question: Is clinically important albuminuria present?
steps.expected_finding: An ACR of 3 to 70 mg/mmol should be confirmed on a subsequent early-morning sample; an initial ACR of 70 mg/mmol or more does not require repeat confirmation.
steps.decision_rationale: Albuminuria is required with GFR category to classify CKD and informs referral and management.
steps.timeframe: At initial CKD assessment; confirm 3 to 70 mg/mmol using an early-morning sample

steps.clinical_question: Does the person meet a risk-based specialist-referral threshold?
steps.expected_finding: A 5-year risk of needing renal replacement therapy above 5% is one NICE referral criterion.
steps.decision_rationale: Risk prediction supplements eGFR, ACR, haematuria, blood pressure and rate-of-decline criteria.
steps.timeframe: Use in adults with CKD stages G3a to G5 when making referral decisions

content.title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
content.specialty: Internal Medicine, Respiratory Medicine and Infectious Diseases

pathophysiology.summary: Community-acquired pneumonia is infection of the distal airways and alveoli acquired outside hospital or early after admission. Alveolar inflammation and exudate impair ventilation and gas exchange; systemic inflammatory effects may cause sepsis and organ dysfunction.
keyMechanisms: Pathogen aspiration or inhalation overcomes airway and innate immune defences.
Alveolar neutrophilic inflammation and fluid cause consolidation and ventilation-perfusion mismatch.
Host response varies with age, comorbidity, immune status and pathogen virulence.
Complications include parapneumonic effusion, empyema, lung abscess, respiratory failure and sepsis.

symptoms: Acute cough with or without sputum
Fever, rigors or malaise
Dyspnoea or pleuritic chest pain
Confusion or functional decline, especially in older adults
physicalSigns: Tachypnoea, hypoxaemia or increased work of breathing
Focal crackles, bronchial breathing or dullness to percussion
Fever or hypothermia with tachycardia
Confusion, hypotension or poor perfusion in severe disease
redFlags: Respiratory failure, exhaustion or rapidly increasing oxygen need
Shock, altered mental status, oliguria or other sepsis-associated organ dysfunction
Multilobar disease, cavitation or a large pleural effusion
Immunocompromise, aspiration risk or failure to improve on appropriate initial therapy

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abrupt pleuritic pain or dyspnoea, thrombosis risk and limited infective prodrome; imaging shows vascular rather than air-space disease.
Orthopnoea, bilateral congestion, raised jugular venous pressure and cardiac dysfunction.
Diffuse upper-respiratory features without focal consolidation or compatible chest imaging.
Subacute constitutional symptoms, epidemiologic risk, upper-lobe or cavitary change and specific microbiology.

content.title: Deep-Vein Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism
content.specialty: Emergency Medicine, Internal Medicine and Haematology

pathophysiology.summary: Venous thromboembolism results from venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. A deep-vein thrombus may obstruct limb venous return or embolise to pulmonary arteries, increasing dead space and pulmonary vascular resistance and, in severe cases, causing right-ventricular failure and shock.
keyMechanisms: Thrombus formation is promoted by immobility, surgery, cancer, oestrogen exposure, pregnancy and inherited or acquired thrombophilia.
Pulmonary arterial obstruction produces ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxaemia.
Acute right-ventricular pressure overload can reduce left-ventricular filling and systemic cardiac output.
Residual venous obstruction and valve damage contribute to post-thrombotic syndrome; persistent vascular obstruction may cause chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

symptoms: Unilateral leg pain or swelling
Sudden unexplained dyspnoea
Pleuritic chest pain, cough, haemoptysis or syncope
Reduced exercise tolerance with recent immobility, surgery, cancer or prior thrombosis
physicalSigns: Unilateral pitting oedema, calf asymmetry or deep venous tenderness
Tachycardia, tachypnoea or hypoxaemia
Signs of right-heart strain such as raised jugular venous pressure
Hypotension or poor perfusion in high-risk pulmonary embolism
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability, syncope with persistent hypotension or obstructive-shock features
Severe hypoxaemia, rapidly escalating oxygen requirement or cardiac arrest
Threatened limb with massive swelling, cyanosis or severe pain
Active major bleeding or another absolute barrier to anticoagulation in a patient with confirmed or highly suspected VTE

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Superficial erythema, warmth and a possible portal of entry with inflammatory features rather than isolated deep venous tenderness.
Posterior knee pathology with fluid tracking into the calf and diagnostic ultrasound findings.
Pressure-type pain, ischaemic electrocardiographic change or a coronary biomarker pattern rather than pleuritic pain and right-heart strain.
Focal infective symptoms or unilateral absent breath sounds with confirmatory chest imaging.

regimens.indication: Fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion for adult diabetic ketoacidosis
regimens.patientGroup: Adults meeting biochemical DKA criteria; use specialist adjustment for pregnancy, renal failure, heart failure, older age and young adults
regimens.dose: 0.1 units/kg/hour, prepared as 50 units soluble human insulin in 50 mL 0.9% sodium chloride
regimens.duration: Continue until ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH is above 7.3, with clinical review and safe transition to subcutaneous insulin
adjustments: Continue the person's long-acting basal insulin at the usual dose and time.
When glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, start 10% glucose and consider reducing the fixed-rate infusion to 0.05 units/kg/hour.
Escalate if ketones are not falling by at least 0.5 mmol/L/hour or bicarbonate is not rising by at least 3 mmol/L/hour.
monitoring: Venous pH, bicarbonate and potassium at 60 minutes, 2 hours and every 2 hours thereafter.
Laboratory electrolytes at least every 4 hours and continuous clinical assessment of fluid balance.

Review gaps: This March 2023 UK professional guideline predates the 2024 international hyperglycaemic-crises consensus and requires reconciliation with that consensus and the current Saudi emergency, endocrine and critical-care protocol before approval. The source advises cautious fluid replacement in ages 18 to 25, older people, pregnancy, heart failure and renal failure. Exact contraindications are not provided as a complete set; local prescribing and infusion safeguards are mandatory. Paediatric DKA is outside scope. Capillary glucose, blood ketones and venous blood gas: All three domains establish hyperglycaemia or diabetes, ketosis and metabolic acidosis.; Immediately at presentation
Hourly capillary glucose and ketones: Ketone clearance, rather than glucose alone, is the principal marker of insulin response.; Hourly during active treatment
Venous pH, bicarbonate, potassium and serum electrolytes: Insulin and fluid therapy can rapidly change potassium and acid-base status.; At 60 minutes, 2 hours, then every 2 hours; laboratory electrolytes every 4 hours
